front: Which cells transmit visual signals from the retina to the brain?
back:
**Ganglion cells**

Ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve; the pathway is photoreceptor → bipolar → ganglion.

front: Which lobes process vision, hearing, and touch?
back: Occipital (vision), temporal (hearing), parietal (somatosensation).

front: Which of the following best describes perceptual set?
back:
**A predisposition to perceive things in a particular way**

Expectations, context, and culture shape interpretation of ambiguous stimuli.

front: Which receptors serve kinesthesia, and what does each monitor?
back: Muscle spindles monitor muscle length and stretch; Golgi tendon organs monitor muscle tension; joint capsule receptors signal joint position. Together they support proprioception without visual input.

front: Which two interaural cues localize sound, and which brainstem structure first compares them?
back: Interaural time differences (best for low frequencies) and interaural intensity/level differences (high frequencies, via the head shadow). The superior olive in the brainstem performs the first binaural comparison.

front: Why are rods more sensitive in dim light but poorer at acuity than cones?
back: Many rods converge onto a single bipolar/ganglion cell, summing weak signals (high sensitivity) but blurring their source (low acuity). Cones show little convergence, giving the reverse tradeoff.

front: Why do the borders between adjacent gray bands look exaggerated, and which retinal cells produce this?
back: Lateral inhibition: horizontal and amacrine cells let an active receptor suppress its neighbors, so responses are amplified at edges. This produces Mach bands and the Hermann grid, and it is why the visual system encodes contrast rather than absolute light intensity.

front: Why does stubbing a toe produce sharp then dull pain? Name the fiber types.
back: Myelinated A-delta fibers conduct fast, sharp, well-localized first pain; unmyelinated C fibers conduct slow, dull, burning second pain. Both are free nerve endings (nociceptors).

front: Why does the fovea have the highest visual acuity?
back: It contains only cones with very low convergence — each foveal cone connects to roughly its own bipolar and ganglion cell, preserving fine spatial detail. Rods are absent there, which is why dim stars vanish when viewed directly.

front: Why is the two-point threshold tiny on fingertips but huge on the back?
back: Receptor density and cortical representation differ: fingertips have dense mechanoreceptors with small receptive fields and large somatosensory cortex area; the back has sparse receptors with large fields, so nearby points merge.

front: You group an array of dots into columns because dots in each column share a color. Which gestalt principle — and which one would grouping by nearness be?
back: Grouping by shared color is similarity; grouping by nearness is proximity. Continuity (preferring smooth continuous lines) and common fate (elements moving together group together) round out the core set.

front: {{c1::Deindividuation}} = anonymity plus arousal and diffused responsibility, producing reduced self-awareness and disinhibited, group-norm-driven behavior.
back: Hooded participants in Zimbardo's shock study delivered longer shocks than identifiable ones. Deindividuation does not make people randomly antisocial; it makes them hyper-responsive to the local group norm (crowds, riots, online anonymity).

front: {{c1::Kin selection}} explains helping relatives through inclusive fitness; {{c2::reciprocal altruism}} (Trivers) explains helping nonkin who can repay later.
back: Reciprocal altruism requires repeated interaction, individual recognition, and cost low relative to benefit, and it is destabilized by cheating, hence cheater detection and reputation. Neither mechanism requires conscious calculation; both are ultimate rather than proximate explanations.

front: {{c1::Lowballing}} secures commitment and then raises the cost; {{c2::foot-in-the-door}} escalates from a small request via self-perception.
back: Lowball: agree to a car price, then fees appear, yet commitment holds. Foot-in-the-door: agreeing to a small favor shifts self-image ('I'm helpful'), raising compliance with a larger one. Door-in-the-face instead works by reciprocal concessions after refusing a huge request.

front: {{c1::Self-handicapping}} means creating an obstacle in advance so that failure can be attributed {{c2::externally}} while success is credited doubly.
back: A student who fears failing stays out late before an exam, protecting self-esteem under the discounting and augmenting principles of attribution. It is a costly self-protective strategy because it genuinely lowers performance to preserve a favorable self-image.

front: {{c1::Social exchange}} theory says relationships persist when rewards exceed costs; {{c2::equity}} theory adds that being over-benefited also distresses.
back: Exchange theory evaluates outcomes against a comparison level (what one expects) and a comparison level for alternatives (what else is available), which is why people stay in poor relationships with worse options. Equity theory predicts restoration attempts by both under- and over-benefited partners.

front: A {{c1::stereotype}} is the cognitive belief about a group, {{c2::prejudice}} is the affective evaluation, and discrimination is the behavior.
back: The three can dissociate: LaPiere found prejudiced attitudes without discriminatory behavior, and institutional rules can produce discrimination with no individual prejudice at all. On test items, ask whether the stem describes a thought, a feeling, or an action.

front: A cancer patient who compares herself with sicker patients feels better; comparing with healthier ones motivates but distresses. Name the theory.
back: Festinger's social comparison theory: absent objective standards, people evaluate themselves against others. Downward comparison protects mood and self-esteem; upward comparison supplies information and motivation but can threaten self-evaluation. Both are common in adjusting to illness.

front: A clinician reports egalitarian views yet shows faster pairing of one race with negative words on the IAT. What does this show, and what is the caveat?
back: Implicit and explicit attitudes are dissociable, and implicit measures capture automatic associations absorbed from the culture. The caveat is psychometric: individual IAT scores have modest test-retest reliability and weakly predict a given person's behavior, so the tool suits group research, not diagnosis.

front: A fundraiser first asks for a 500 dollar gift, is refused, then asks for 50 and gets it. Name the technique and its two mechanisms.
back: Door-in-the-face: the refused large request makes the small one look like a concession, engaging reciprocal concession and perceptual contrast. It requires the same requester and a short delay, unlike foot-in-the-door, which works through self-perception after an initial small yes.

front: A patient told firmly that he must quit smoking becomes more insistent on his right to smoke. Name the phenomenon and the counseling implication.
back: Psychological reactance (Brehm): a perceived threat to behavioral freedom motivates restoring it, often by doing the forbidden thing. Motivational interviewing avoids reactance by eliciting the patient's own reasons for change and explicitly affirming autonomy over the decision.

front: Allport's contact hypothesis names four conditions under which contact reduces prejudice. What are they?
back: Equal status within the situation, common goals, intergroup cooperation rather than competition, and support from authorities, law, or custom. Meta-analyses find contact reduces prejudice even without all four, but effects are substantially larger when the conditions are met.

front: Asch's effect was mostly {{c1::normative}} influence (public compliance, private disbelief); Sherif's autokinetic norms show {{c2::informational}} influence.
back: Asch's participants knew the majority was wrong but avoided standing out; conformity fell with private answers. In Sherif's ambiguous autokinetic task, group norms were internalized and persisted when tested alone up to a year later.

front: At Robbers Cave, hostility between two boys' camps fell only when they had to repair a shared water supply. What theory and remedy does this illustrate?
back: Realistic conflict theory: competition over scarce resources generates intergroup hostility. Mere contact did not help; superordinate goals requiring genuine cooperation did. Criticisms include a tiny homogeneous sample and heavy experimenter involvement in provoking the conflict.

front: Berkowitz's revision: frustration causes aggression only via {{c1::negative affect}}, and aggressive cues such as guns ({{c2::the weapons effect}}) amplify it.
back: The original frustration-aggression hypothesis said frustration always precedes aggression. Berkowitz reframed it: any aversive event (pain, heat, insult) creates negative affect that primes aggression, and situational cues like visible weapons increase aggressive responding.

front: Boys assigned to groups by a coin flip still allocated more money to their own group. Name the paradigm and the theory it supports.
back: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm, supporting social identity theory: people derive self-esteem from group membership, so they favor the in-group even when the category is arbitrary and there is no competition or history. In-group favoritism, not out-group hostility, is the usual first result.

front: Central-route persuasion requires both {{c1::motivation}} and {{c2::ability}} to elaborate, and it produces durable, behavior-predictive attitude change.
back: In the elaboration likelihood model, careful processing of argument quality (central route) yields attitudes resistant to counterargument. Peripheral-route change from surface cues is weaker and temporary.

front: Cialdini's six principles of influence: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, {{c1::social proof}}, authority, liking, and {{c2::scarcity}}.
back: Each maps to a technique: reciprocity to the free sample, consistency to foot-in-the-door, social proof to 'most patients choose this', authority to the white coat, liking to rapport building, and scarcity to limited-time offers. All are peripheral-route levers.

front: Dissonance can be reduced by changing the {{c1::behavior}}, changing or adding {{c2::cognitions}}, or trivializing the inconsistency.
back: A smoker can quit (behavior), decide the evidence is weak or that smoking controls weight (add consonant cognitions), or decide health risks are overblown (trivialize). Dissonance is an aversive arousal state, strongest when the behavior is freely chosen.

front: Distinguish conformity, compliance, and obedience.
back:
**Conformity**: matching attitudes/behavior to a **group norm** (Asch).
**Compliance**: changing behavior due to a **direct request** (foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face).
**Obedience**: following a **direct order** from an authority (Milgram).
hint: Conformity = group; compliance = request; obedience = command.

front: Distinguish discrimination, prejudice, and ethnocentrism in social terms.
back:
**Prejudice**: a (negative) attitude toward a group.
**Discrimination**: differential treatment/action against a group.
**Ethnocentrism**: judging another culture by the standards of one's own (seeing one's own as superior).
**Cultural relativism**: judging a culture by its own standards.
hint: Ethnocentrism = "my culture is the standard"; relativism = judge on own terms.

front: Distinguish dispositional from situational attribution and the self-serving bias.
back:
**Dispositional (internal)**: behavior caused by personality/character.
**Situational (external)**: behavior caused by environment/circumstances.

**Self-serving bias**: attribute our **successes** to internal factors and our **failures** to external ones.
hint: Self-serving: my wins = me; my losses = the situation.

front: Distinguish social facilitation from social loafing.
back:
**Social facilitation**: presence of others **improves** performance on simple/well-learned tasks (and worsens complex ones).

**Social loafing**: individuals exert **less effort** in a group than alone, because individual contribution isn't identifiable.
hint: Facilitation = others boost easy tasks; loafing = slacking in a group.

front: Festinger and Carlsmith (1959): what was the design, and which group changed its attitude?
back: After a boring peg-turning task, participants were paid $1 or $20 to tell the next subject it was fun. The $1 group later rated the task as more enjoyable: insufficient justification produced dissonance, resolved by changing the attitude. $20 provided external justification, so no change.

front: Group polarization works through {{c1::persuasive arguments}} (hearing novel points favoring the lean) and {{c2::social comparison}} (outdoing the group norm).
back: Discussion among like-minded people shifts the group mean toward a more extreme version of its initial lean, producing risky or cautious shifts, jury extremity, and echo-chamber effects online.

front: Hamilton's rule: altruism toward kin evolves when {{c1::rB > C}}, the benefit weighted by genetic relatedness exceeding the cost to the helper.
back: Kin selection explains why helping tracks relatedness (more aid to siblings than cousins). Reciprocal altruism extends helping to non-kin when repayment is likely, in stable groups with individual recognition.

front: How does Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis differ from egoistic accounts of helping?
back: Batson: empathic concern produces truly altruistic helping, persisting even when escape from the distressing scene is easy. Egoistic rivals say we help to relieve our own discomfort (negative-state relief, arousal cost-reward) or for expected reciprocity.

front: In Asch's variations, what most sharply reduced conformity?
back: A single dissenter, even an inaccurate one, cut conformity to roughly 5-9%. Writing answers privately also reduced it, and increasing majority size raised conformity only up to a plateau around 3-5 confederates.

front: In Bandura's 1965 follow-up, what did vicarious punishment change, and what did incentives reveal?
back: Children who saw the model punished spontaneously imitated less than those who saw reward or no consequence. But when all children were offered incentives to reproduce the acts, groups performed equally: consequences affected performance, not learning.

front: In ELM experiments, what variable flips people from peripheral to central processing?
back: Personal relevance (involvement). Told a tuition policy would apply at their own school next year, students were persuaded by argument quality; told it applied elsewhere or far in the future, they followed cues like source expertise instead.

front: In the {{c1::sleeper}} effect, a message from a discredited source gains influence over time because {{c2::source memory}} fades faster than the message.
back: Initially the discounting cue suppresses persuasion, but weeks later the message is remembered while its dubious source is forgotten, so attitude change emerges. It requires the message and discounting cue to be dissociated in memory.

front: Kelley's covariation model: high {{c1::consensus}}, high {{c2::distinctiveness}}, and high consistency point to a situational (external) attribution.
back: If everyone laughs at this comedian (consensus), Maria laughs only at this one (distinctiveness), and she always does (consistency), the cause is the comedian. Low consensus plus low distinctiveness plus high consistency yields a dispositional attribution.

front: Latane and Darley's helping sequence: notice the event, {{c1::interpret it as an emergency}}, {{c2::take responsibility}}, know how to help, then act.
back: Pluralistic ignorance blocks the interpretation step: in the smoke-filled room study, 75% reported smoke when alone versus about 10% with two passive confederates, because everyone read everyone else's calm as evidence nothing was wrong.

front: Milgram obedience fell to about {{c1::30}}% with touch proximity and about {{c2::20}}% when the experimenter gave orders by phone.
back: Situational variations mattered more than personality: two rebelling peers cut full obedience to 10%, while merely reading the word pairs as another person pressed the switch raised it to 92.5%. Physical and authority proximity drive obedience.

front: Repeated, unreinforced exposure to a stimulus increases liking, an effect named {{c1::mere exposure}} and demonstrated by {{c2::Zajonc}}.
back: It is strongest for initially neutral or mildly positive stimuli, occurs even with subliminal exposures, and can reverse with overexposure or with initially disliked stimuli. It is a peripheral-route mechanism behind advertising repetition and behind familiarity in attraction.

front: Same crowd, opposite effects: when does the presence of others improve versus worsen your performance?
back: Facilitation: your output is individually evaluated and the task is simple or well-practiced. Loafing: outputs are pooled and unidentifiable, so effort drops. Impairment: you are evaluated but the task is complex or novel, so arousal strengthens wrong dominant responses.

front: Stereotype threat impairs performance by loading {{c1::working memory}} with anxiety and monitoring; reduced by {{c2::self-affirmation}} and role models.
back: The fear of confirming a negative group stereotype consumes cognitive resources. It affects any negatively stereotyped group on a relevant task (women in math, whites vs Asians in math) and is eased by reframing tests, affirming values, and counter-stereotypic role models.

front: Subjects who guess a study's hypothesis behave so as to confirm it. Name this threat and the design features that control it.
back: Demand characteristics. Controls are blinding participants to condition and hypothesis using cover stories and placebo controls, plus keeping experimenters blind, since experimenter expectancy leaks through subtle cues. Together these define the double-blind design.

front: Teachers told that certain randomly chosen students were late bloomers saw those students gain more on later testing. Name the effect and its mediator.
back: The Pygmalion effect (Rosenthal and Jacobson), an expectancy effect operating as a self-fulfilling prophecy: expectations changed teacher warmth, feedback, and opportunities offered, which changed performance. It is a core reason blinding is required in research designs.

front: The {{c1::actor-observer}} bias: we attribute our own behavior to the situation but others' identical behavior to their disposition.
back: Explained by perceptual salience (we see our situation; observers see us) and information differences. The asymmetry shrinks or reverses for positive outcomes, where the self-serving bias takes over.

front: The {{c1::halo}} effect spreads one positive trait to unrelated judgments; its mirror image is the {{c2::horns}} effect.
back: Interviewers rate attractive applicants as more intelligent and more ethical, a case called the physical attractiveness stereotype. In clinical settings the same bias distorts judgments of a patient's adherence, credibility about pain, and likely follow-through on a plan.

front: The {{c1::ultimate attribution error}} extends the FAE to groups: outgroup failures reflect disposition, outgroup successes reflect luck or special advantage.
back: Pettigrew's group-level bias: negative outgroup acts are seen as 'the kind of people they are,' while positive acts are explained away situationally. It maintains stereotypes despite disconfirming evidence.

front: The tendency to attribute others' behavior to disposition while excusing our own as situational is the {{c1::fundamental attribution error}} (with the {{c2::actor-observer}} asymmetry).
back: FAE: overweighting personality for others; actor-observer bias: situational excuses for ourselves.

front: What are classic peripheral cues in persuasion, and when do they dominate?
back: Source attractiveness, credibility or expertise labels, number of arguments, music, and positive mood. They dominate when personal relevance is low, the audience is distracted or tired, or need for cognition is low, so no one scrutinizes argument quality.

front: What are stereotype threat and the self-fulfilling prophecy?
back:
**Stereotype threat**: anxiety about confirming a negative stereotype about one's group **impairs performance**.

**Self-fulfilling prophecy**: an expectation about someone causes behavior that makes the expectation come true (e.g., Pygmalion/Rosenthal effect).
hint: Stereotype threat = fear of confirming → worse performance.

front: What are the antecedents and hallmark symptoms of groupthink (Janis)?
back: Antecedents: high cohesion, directive leader, isolation from outside views, stress. Symptoms: illusions of invulnerability and unanimity, self-censorship, mindguards, stereotyped outgroups. Classic case: Bay of Pigs. Remedies: assigned devil's advocate, leader withholds opinion, outside experts.

front: What are the key numbers from Asch's line-judgment conformity study?
back: About 76% of participants conformed to the wrong majority at least once; conformity occurred on about 37% of all critical trials (the majority answered wrong on 12 of 18 trials). Control participants alone erred less than 1% of the time.

front: What are the main criticisms of Milgram's obedience studies?
back: Ethical: deception, severe stress, and a compromised right to withdraw (the prods pressured continuation). Methodological: demand characteristics and trust that the experimenter would allow no real harm. Still, Burger's 2009 partial replication found about 70% compliance at the 150-volt point.

front: What behavioral consequence does the just-world hypothesis predict?
back: Victim-blaming: believing people get what they deserve, observers derogate assault victims, the poor, or the ill to preserve the comforting belief that the world is fair, especially when they cannot compensate the victim.

front: What biological correlates accompany aggression, and how do hostile and instrumental aggression differ?
back: Low serotonin activity, higher testosterone, amygdala hyperreactivity, and reduced prefrontal regulation correlate with aggression. Hostile aggression is impulsive and anger-driven with harm as the goal; instrumental aggression is calculated, using harm as a means to another end.

front: What did Asch's conformity study demonstrate?
back:
**Conformity**: participants gave obviously wrong answers (line-length task) to match a unanimous group.

Shows **normative social influence** — conforming to be accepted/fit in, even against clear evidence. Conformity dropped sharply with even one dissenting ally.
hint: Asch = line study = conformity to group (normative influence).

front: What did LaPiere's 1934 study show, and when do attitudes actually predict behavior?
back: Touring the US with a Chinese couple, LaPiere was refused service once, yet over 90% of the same establishments later wrote that they would refuse Chinese guests: a large attitude-behavior gap. Attitudes predict behavior when specific, strong, accessible, formed by direct experience, and social pressure is low.

front: What did Milgram's obedience study show?
back:
Participants delivered what they believed were dangerous "shocks" because an **authority figure** instructed them.

Demonstrated high **obedience to authority** even against personal conscience. Obedience = compliance with a direct command from an authority.
hint: Milgram = shocks = obedience to authority.

front: What did Steele and Aronson's 1995 stereotype threat experiments show?
back: Black students underperformed white students on difficult verbal items framed as diagnostic of intellectual ability, but the gap vanished when the same items were framed as a nondiagnostic problem-solving task. Merely making race salient before the test also depressed performance.

front: What did Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment illustrate?
back:
Ordinary students assigned "guard" or "prisoner" roles rapidly adopted abusive/submissive behaviors.

Illustrates the power of **social roles, situational forces, and deindividuation** to shape behavior, overriding individual disposition.
hint: Zimbardo = prison roles = power of the situation/roles.

front: What factors increase interpersonal attraction?
back:
**Proximity** (mere exposure effect — familiarity breeds liking), **similarity** (shared attitudes), **physical attractiveness** (halo effect), and **reciprocity** of liking.

Mere exposure: repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking.
hint: Proximity, similarity, attractiveness, reciprocity. Familiarity → liking.

front: What happened in the Stanford Prison Experiment, and why is it now heavily criticized?
back: Planned for 14 days, it ended after 6: 'guards' became abusive and several 'prisoners' broke down, illustrating role internalization and situational power. Criticisms: Zimbardo acted as warden and coached guards, demand characteristics, self-selection in the 'prison life' ad, and a tiny sample.

front: What is cognitive dissonance and how is it resolved?
back:
The **mental discomfort** from holding two conflicting cognitions or acting against one's beliefs (Festinger).

Resolved by **changing the attitude or behavior** to restore consistency (e.g., "I did boring work for \$1, so it must have been fun" — justification).
hint: Discomfort from inconsistency → change attitude to match behavior.

front: What is effort justification, and what is the classic evidence for it?
back: Aronson and Mills: women who underwent a severe (embarrassing) initiation to join a discussion group rated the same boring discussion more attractive than mild-initiation or control groups. Suffering for something creates dissonance resolved by valuing it more; basis of hazing effects.

front: What is group polarization and groupthink?
back:
**Group polarization**: group discussion **strengthens** the members' initial leaning toward a more extreme position.

**Groupthink**: desire for harmony/conformity in a group leads to **poor decision-making** by suppressing dissent and realistic appraisal.
hint: Polarization = group goes more extreme; groupthink = harmony kills good decisions.

front: What is the bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility?
back:
**Bystander effect**: the more people present, the **less likely** any one person helps in an emergency.

Due to **diffusion of responsibility** (everyone assumes someone else will act) and pluralistic ignorance. (Darley & Latané, after the Kitty Genovese case.)
hint: More bystanders = less help (responsibility is diffused).

front: What is the difference between an in-group and out-group, and in-group bias?
back:
**In-group**: a group one identifies with ("us").
**Out-group**: a group one is not part of ("them").

**In-group bias**: favoring one's own group. **Out-group homogeneity**: perceiving out-group members as "all the same."
hint: In-group = us (favored); out-group = them (seen as all alike).

front: What is the fundamental attribution error?
back:
The tendency to **overemphasize dispositional (personality) explanations** and underemphasize situational ones **when judging others' behavior**.

We blame their character but excuse our own behavior on circumstances (the actor-observer bias).
hint: Judging others: "they're a bad person" (disposition) over "tough situation."

front: What is the pattern and function of the self-serving bias, and when does it reverse?
back: People take internal credit for successes and blame failures on external causes, protecting self-esteem. It is weakened or reversed in depression and in some collectivist cultures, where self-effacing attributions are normative.

front: What is the Ringelmann rope-pulling effect, and what conditions eliminate it?
back: Individual effort drops as group size grows (social loafing): pooled output and low identifiability reduce motivation. It shrinks when contributions are identifiable, the task matters, or the group is cohesive, and it is larger in individualist cultures and among men.

front: What were Milgram's baseline obedience findings?
back: 65% of participants (26 of 40) continued to the maximum 450 volts, and every participant went to at least 300 volts. Psychiatrists had predicted fewer than 1% would fully obey. Obedience was to an experimenter's escalating verbal prods.

front: What were the key numbers in Darley and Latane's seizure (bystander) study?
back: Participants who believed they alone heard a seizure helped 85% of the time and fastest; with four other presumed bystanders, only 31% helped by the end. Diffusion of responsibility, prompted by the Kitty Genovese case, not apathy, explained the drop.

front: What were the outcomes of Bandura's 1961 Bobo doll experiment?
back: Children who watched an adult beat the Bobo doll imitated the specific novel physical and verbal aggressive acts far more than controls; boys showed more physical aggression, and same-sex models were imitated more. Aggression was learned by observation, with no reinforcement to the child.

front: When does Bem's self-perception theory explain attitude change better than dissonance theory?
back: When prior attitudes are weak, ambiguous, or novel: people simply infer attitudes from their behavior, with no arousal needed. Dissonance requires aversive arousal, shown by misattribution studies where blaming arousal on a pill eliminated attitude change.

front: Which situational factors increase helping, and what did the Good Samaritan seminary study show?
back: Good mood, perceived similarity to the victim, rural or low-density settings, modeling, and low time pressure. Darley and Batson: only 10% of hurried seminary students helped a slumped stranger versus 63% of unhurried ones, even when lecturing on the Good Samaritan.

front: Zajonc: an audience strengthens the {{c1::dominant}} response, improving {{c2::easy or well-learned}} tasks and impairing difficult ones.
back: Social facilitation via arousal: even cockroaches ran simple mazes faster and complex mazes slower with an audience. In humans, evaluation apprehension and distraction-conflict add to mere presence.

front: {{c1::Acculturative stress}} is the ongoing strain of adapting to a new culture, distinct from the brief disorientation of {{c2::culture shock}}.
back: Berry's model gives four strategies: integration, with the best outcomes, assimilation, separation, and marginalization, with the worst. Acculturative stress is linked to depression and helps explain why the immigrant health advantage erodes across generations.

front: {{c1::Anticipatory}} socialization is rehearsing the norms of a future role, e.g., a premed shadowing physicians or an engaged couple cohabiting.
back: Anticipatory socialization eases role transitions by adopting a reference group's values in advance. Merton tied it to reference group theory: we orient toward groups we aspire to join.

front: {{c1::Assimilation}} is a minority absorbing the dominant culture, losing distinctiveness; {{c2::amalgamation}} melts groups into a genuinely new culture.
back: Assimilation is one-directional (A plus B become A); amalgamation is the true melting pot (A plus B become D, a new blend). Multiculturalism instead keeps groups distinct and coequal.

front: {{c1::Cultural diffusion}} spreads elements between societies (yoga to the West); {{c2::cultural transmission}} passes culture down generations within one.
back: Diffusion moves objects, ideas, and practices across cultural boundaries via trade, migration, and media; globalization accelerates it. Transmission (via family, school, religion) is how each generation inherits its culture.

front: {{c1::Cultural lag}} (Ogburn): material culture changes faster than nonmaterial culture, e.g., laws and ethics trailing genetic testing technology.
back: William Ogburn coined cultural lag for the gap when technology outpaces the norms governing it — organ allocation after transplantation, privacy norms after social media. The lag produces social problems until norms catch up.

front: {{c1::Culture shock}} is the disorientation felt when immersed in an unfamiliar culture whose taken-for-granted norms no longer apply.
back: Culture shock reveals how deeply norms are internalized: greetings, personal space, food, and time norms suddenly fail. It typically eases through adjustment and adaptation phases.

front: {{c1::Folkways}} are everyday norms of custom and politeness; violations (facing backward in an elevator) draw only mild disapproval.
back: Sumner's hierarchy of norms: folkways (etiquette), mores (moral weight), taboos (unthinkable). Folkway violations make you odd, not immoral — wearing pajamas to class versus stealing.

front: {{c1::Material}} culture is a society's physical objects (tools, dress, buildings); {{c2::nonmaterial}} culture is its values, beliefs, norms, and language.
back: Material culture is tangible; nonmaterial culture is the ideas behind it. The two interact: the smartphone (material) reshapes norms of communication (nonmaterial), and lag between them causes friction.

front: {{c1::Mores}} are morally significant norms drawing strong sanctions; {{c2::taboos}} are so deep that violation evokes revulsion, e.g., incest or cannibalism.
back: Mores often become law (theft, assault); violating them makes one immoral, not merely rude. Taboos are the strongest category, provoking disgust and expulsion across nearly all societies.

front: {{c1::Multiculturalism}} (pluralism) endorses distinct cultures coexisting with equal standing — the 'salad bowl' rather than the melting pot.
back: Under pluralism, groups retain languages, religions, and traditions while sharing civic life, e.g., Switzerland's language communities. It contrasts with assimilationist policies that pressure conformity.

front: {{c1::Prescriptive}} norms state what one should do; {{c2::proscriptive}} norms state what one must not do, and are usually enforced more forcefully.
back: Both are backed by sanctions, formal or informal. Handwashing before an exam is prescriptive; the prohibition on dating patients is proscriptive. Mores and taboos are almost always proscriptive, which is why their violation draws the strongest reaction.

front: {{c1::Primary}} socialization is early childhood learning of basic norms in the family; {{c2::secondary}} socialization occurs later in schools and workplaces.
back: Anticipatory socialization rehearses a role not yet held, and resocialization strips an old identity to install a new one, most intensely inside total institutions. Reverse socialization runs upward, as when children teach parents new technology or new norms.

front: {{c1::Resocialization}} is discarding old behaviors and identities to adopt new ones, most intensely inside total institutions like boot camp or prison.
back: Resocialization is usually deliberate and often involuntary: military training, prisons, cults, psychiatric commitment. It typically begins by breaking down the old identity, then rebuilding via rewards and punishments.

front: {{c1::Sanctions}} enforce norms and can be positive or negative, formal (a fine, a diploma) or informal (a smile, gossip, ostracism).
back: Sanctions are the enforcement arm of social control. Formal sanctions come from institutions with official authority; informal sanctions arise in everyday interaction and are often the more constant regulators.

front: {{c1::Sex}} refers to biological characteristics and {{c2::gender}} to socially constructed roles; gender identity is internal, orientation is attraction.
back: All four vary independently, so knowing one predicts the others only statistically. Treating gender as socially constructed does not make it less real in its effects, since it structures opportunity, expectation, and treatment throughout life.

front: A {{c1::subculture}} has distinct norms within the mainstream (e.g., med students); a {{c2::counterculture}} opposes dominant values (e.g., 1960s hippies).
back: Subcultures (gamers, regional groups, professions) differentiate without rejecting society. Countercultures (1960s hippies, revolutionary movements) define themselves in opposition to dominant norms and may seek change.

front: A {{c1::total institution}} (Goffman) controls every aspect of residents' lives — prisons, asylums, boot camps — cut off from wider society.
back: Goffman's Asylums (1961): total institutions batch daily life under one authority, strip prior identity through mortification (uniforms, head shaving, new names), and rebuild the self to institutional specifications.

front: A patient describes an ataque de nervios after a family loss. What is a cultural concept of distress, and how should it be handled clinically?
back: It is a symptom cluster recognized as an illness within a specific culture, with locally shared meaning and expected course. DSM-5 reframes these as cultural concepts of distress and supplies a Cultural Formulation Interview; they are treated as genuine distress rather than dismissed as folklore.

front: A physician's technical vocabulary leaves a patient nodding without understanding. Analyze this using culture and socialization concepts.
back: Medicine functions as a subculture with its own argot, and command of that argot marks completed professional socialization and, in Bourdieu's terms, cultural capital. The mismatch produces functionally low health literacy in the encounter; teach-back is the standard corrective.

front: Classify: a hospital forbids staff from accepting gifts; a nurse who does is fired. Folkway, more, or taboo?
back: A more (formalized into policy): the rule carries moral weight about integrity and trust, and violation brings serious sanction. Folkway violations would draw only disapproval; taboos evoke visceral revulsion.

front: Contrast norms, mores, and folkways.
back: Norms are general rules; mores carry strong moral weight; folkways are everyday customs with mild sanctions.

front: Define cultural capital.
back: Non-financial assets — knowledge, tastes, credentials, manners — that confer social mobility and advantage.

front: Define socialization and its two phases.
back: Learning society's norms and values. Primary occurs in childhood (family); secondary continues through life (school, work).

front: Dependency theory argues underdevelopment results from:
back:
**Exploitation by wealthy nations**

A direct critique of modernization theory.

front: Display rules refer to:
back:
**Cultural norms governing emotional expression**

Cultures differ in when and how strongly emotions may be shown.

front: Distinguish high culture from popular culture.
back: High culture is associated with elites (opera, fine art) and confers distinction; popular culture is mass-consumed (TV, sports, memes). Bourdieu argued tastes for high culture function as cultural capital.

front: Distinguish high-context and low-context communication cultures, and give one clinical implication.
back: High-context communication relies on shared background, indirectness, and nonverbal cues; low-context communication is explicit and literal. A patient from a high-context culture may signal refusal by hesitation rather than saying no, so a direct yes-or-no question can produce false agreement.

front: Distinguish material and non-material culture.
back: Material: physical objects and technology. Non-material: beliefs, values, language, and norms.

front: Hall's {{c1::proxemics}} studies culturally patterned use of personal space; a physical exam routinely enters the {{c2::intimate}} zone.
back: Hall described intimate, personal, social, and public distances, with norms varying widely across cultures. Eye contact, touch, and silence are patterned the same way, so a patient read as evasive or rude may simply be following a different set of nonverbal rules.

front: Heavy television viewers overestimate crime rates and distrust strangers more than light viewers. Name the theory and its key confound.
back: Gerbner's cultivation theory: sustained exposure to media portrayals shapes beliefs about social reality, producing what he called mean world syndrome. The confound is that the data are correlational, and anxious or homebound people may both watch more and fear more.

front: How can ethnic enclaves affect assimilation?
back: Enclaves (e.g., Chinatowns, Little Havana) supply social capital, jobs, and familiar institutions, easing arrival but potentially slowing linguistic and structural assimilation; second generations typically assimilate faster.

front: How do laws relate to norms?
back: Laws are norms formally codified and enforced by the state, usually derived from mores (assault, theft). Not all mores become law, and some laws outlast the norms that produced them.

front: How does acculturation differ from assimilation?
back: Acculturation is adopting elements of another culture (language, dress) while potentially retaining one's own — it can be two-way. Assimilation is fuller absorption into the dominant culture with loss of distinctiveness.

front: How does religion function as an agent of socialization, and what is one documented health correlate?
back: It transmits values, rituals, and moral boundaries while supplying a reference group and a dense social network. Regular attendance correlates with lower mortality, plausibly through social support, lower substance use, and coping resources, though healthier people also attend more, confounding the estimate.

front: How does the workplace act as an agent of socialization?
back: It resocializes adults into occupational norms — dress, hierarchy, jargon, professional ethics. Medical training is a classic case: students internalize detachment norms and the profession's culture, not just knowledge.

front: Identity is influenced by all EXCEPT:
back:
**Blood type**

Despite popular belief in some cultures, there is no evidence for blood-type personality.

front: Immigrants may speak the new language fluently yet remain excluded from clubs, friendship circles, and intermarriage. Distinguish the two assimilations.
back: Cultural assimilation, or acculturation, is adopting the host culture's language, dress, and customs. Structural assimilation is entry into its primary institutions, friendship networks, and families. Gordon argued the structural step is far harder, and it is where discrimination operates.

front: In {{c1::collectivist}} cultures medical decisions are often family-centered; {{c2::individualist}} cultures center the individual patient's autonomy.
back: This shapes informed consent, disclosure of a terminal diagnosis, and who signs the form. It also moderates attribution, since collectivist samples make fewer dispositional attributions. US bioethics presumes individual autonomy, which can conflict with a family asking that a diagnosis be withheld.

front: In Mead's theory, what are the 'I' and the 'me'?
back: The 'me' is the socialized self — internalized expectations of others; the 'I' is the spontaneous, acting self that responds. The self is the ongoing conversation between them, formed through social interaction.

front: Kleinman's {{c1::explanatory model}} interview asks what the patient thinks caused the illness, its name, its course, and the treatment expected.
back: It surfaces the gap between the clinician's disease framework and the patient's illness experience, a common and correctable driver of nonadherence. It operationalizes cultural humility better than memorizing group traits, which slides into stereotyping.

front: Medical students learn detachment, hierarchy, and what not to say by watching residents rather than from the syllabus. Name both concepts at work.
back: Professional socialization operating through the hidden curriculum: informal norms, role modeling, and the reward structure teach the profession's culture. Classic ethnographies, including Becker's Boys in White and Fox's training for uncertainty, describe how students acquire detached concern.

front: Modernization theory proposes societies develop by:
back:
**Following a path from traditional to industrial**

Criticized as ethnocentric and for ignoring colonial history.

front: Neugarten's {{c1::social clock}} is a culture's expected timetable for life events, so being {{c2::off-time}} itself produces distress.
back: Age norms govern when one should finish school, marry, or retire, and they shift by cohort and culture. Off-time events such as early widowhood or a late first birth are more distressing than on-time ones, which is why chronological age poorly predicts adjustment.

front: One resident washes hands even when unobserved; another only when the attending is watching. Distinguish internalization from mere compliance.
back: Internalization means the norm has become part of the self, so behavior persists without surveillance. Compliance is behavior contingent on sanctions and observation. Effective socialization aims at internalization, which is why safety culture outperforms monitoring alone.

front: Parents describe newborn daughters as delicate and sons as strong despite matched birth records. Name the process and its sociological reading.
back: Gender socialization: agents transmit gender expectations from birth, so observed differences partly reflect differential treatment rather than innate traits. This supports the constructionist claim that gender is continuously produced in interaction, what West and Zimmerman called doing gender.

front: Resocialization is most dramatic in:
back:
**Total institutions like prisons and the military**

Prior identity is deliberately stripped and rebuilt.

front: Role exit involves:
back:
**Disengaging from a role central to identity**

Retirement and divorce are common examples.

front: Socialization is the process by which people:
back:
**Learn the norms and values of their society**

Primary socialization in childhood; secondary continues through life.

front: Some second-generation immigrants advance economically while others assimilate into disadvantaged contexts. Name this model and what predicts each path.
back: Segmented assimilation: outcomes depend on the receiving context, including racial classification, neighborhood, school quality, and the resources of the coethnic community. It explains why straight-line assimilation fails as a universal model and why immigrant health advantages erode across generations.

front: The {{c1::Sapir-Whorf}} hypothesis (linguistic relativity): the language we speak shapes how we perceive and think about the world.
back: The strong version (language determines thought) is rejected; the weak version (language influences habitual perception, e.g., color terms, spatial framing) has empirical support. Central to language's role in culture.

front: What are agents of socialization?
back: Family, schools, peer groups, media, and workplaces — the sources transmitting culture.

front: What are Mead's three stages in developing the self?
back: Preparatory stage: imitation without meaning. Play stage: taking on one role at a time (playing doctor). Game stage: managing multiple roles at once and grasping the generalized other — society's overall expectations.

front: What are the phases of a rite of passage?
back: Separation from the old status, transition (liminality) between statuses, and reincorporation with the new status — van Gennep's scheme. Examples: graduation, boot camp, quinceanera, white-coat ceremonies.

front: What are the three steps of Cooley's looking-glass self?
back: We imagine how we appear to others; we imagine their judgment of that appearance; we develop self-feeling (pride or shame) from the imagined judgment. Self-concept is built from perceived, not actual, appraisals.

front: What do cases of extreme isolation (e.g., Genie) demonstrate about socialization?
back: That the self and language require social interaction: isolated children show profound deficits in speech and attachment, only partly recoverable. Socialization has sensitive periods and is not automatic maturation.

front: What is a cultural universal? Give examples.
back: A practice found in every known society — family units, funeral rites, language, incest prohibitions, music. Murdock cataloged dozens; the forms vary enormously even when the category is universal.

front: What is a degradation ceremony?
back: A ritual that publicly strips a person's identity and assigns a stigmatized one — the intake process of prisons (mug shot, uniform, number). Garfinkel's term; often the entry point of resocialization.

front: What is cultural lag?
back: Non-material culture (norms, laws) adapting more slowly than material culture (technology) changes.

front: What is cultural relativism vs. ethnocentrism?
back: Cultural relativism judges a culture by its own standards; ethnocentrism judges others by one's own culture.

front: What is ethnocentrism's functional side, per some sociologists?
back: In-group pride can strengthen solidarity, loyalty, and cultural continuity. But it also fuels prejudice, conflict, and misjudgment of other groups, so its group-binding function carries clear social costs.

front: What is the difference between assimilation and multiculturalism?
back: Assimilation absorbs minority groups into the dominant culture; multiculturalism preserves distinct identities.

front: What is xenocentrism?
back: Judging one's own culture as inferior to others — the reverse of ethnocentrism — e.g., assuming imported goods, foreign medicine, or another country's institutions are inherently better.

front: What makes something a symbol in the cultural sense?
back: Anything that carries a shared meaning recognized by members of a culture — a flag, a wedding ring, a white coat, a gesture. Meanings are arbitrary, learned, and can differ or offend across cultures.

front: Which socialization agent dominates in adolescence, and what does it uniquely teach?
back: Peer groups: interaction among equals, negotiation, and identity experimentation outside adult supervision. Peer norms can rival family values, which is why adolescence is a peak of conformity pressure.

front: Why does cultural relativism matter in medicine, and where are its limits?
back: Understanding patients' health beliefs in context improves care and trust (e.g., dietary and religious practices). Limits arise when practices cause harm; clinicians balance respect with duties like child protection.

front: Why is language considered the keystone of nonmaterial culture?
back: It stores and transmits accumulated knowledge across generations, enables shared symbols and abstract thought, and (per Sapir-Whorf's weak form) shapes habitual perception. Culture cannot persist without it.

front: {{c1::Bonding}} social capital is dense within-group ties that supply support; {{c2::bridging}} social capital crosses groups and supplies novel information.
back: Bonding ties enforce norms and provide emotional and material help, while bridging ties reach beyond redundant contacts. This is why Granovetter's weak ties deliver job leads: strong ties mostly know what you already know, so opportunity flows across bridges.

front: {{c1::Emotional labor}} (Hochschild) is managing feeling to meet a job's display rules; {{c2::surface}} acting fakes it, deep acting alters the feeling.
back: Surface acting generates the greatest emotional dissonance and predicts burnout and depersonalization among nurses and physicians; deep acting is less depleting. Feeling rules are organizational norms about what one should feel, not merely what one should show.

front: {{c1::Groupthink}} occurs when a cohesive group's desire for consensus suppresses dissent and realistic appraisal, producing bad decisions.
back: Janis's term, illustrated by the Bay of Pigs: illusions of unanimity and invulnerability, self-censorship, pressure on dissenters. Remedies include devil's advocates and soliciting outside opinions.

front: {{c1::Homophily}} is the tendency to form ties with similar others; network {{c2::density}} is the fraction of possible ties that actually exist.
back: High homophily plus high density produces redundant information and strong norm enforcement, which is how behaviors such as smoking, obesity, and vaccination spread through networks. The same structure limits access to new opportunities, which is why weak bridging ties matter.

front: {{c1::Impression management}} is the conscious shaping of how others perceive us — a physician's white coat, steady tone, and framed diplomas.
back: Goffman's term for controlling the definition of the situation: dress, speech, setting, and selective disclosure. Job interviews and first dates are peak impression management; social media extends it online.

front: {{c1::McDonaldization}} (Ritzer): efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control via technology spread from fast food across institutions.
back: Ritzer extended Weber's rationalization: universities (credit hours), medicine (15-minute visits, checklists), and retail adopt the four principles. The 'irrationality of rationality' is dehumanization and lost quality.

front: {{c1::Role conflict}} is tension between roles of two different statuses; {{c2::role strain}} is tension among expectations within a single role.
back: Conflict: a physician-parent paged during a school recital (two statuses collide). Strain: one status with competing demands — a resident expected to be both fast and thorough on a 30-patient service.

front: {{c1::Role exit}} is disengaging from a central role and rebuilding identity — retiring, leaving a religious order, divorcing.
back: Ebaugh's stages: initial doubts, seeking alternatives, a departure turning point, then creating an 'ex' identity. Old roles linger, and others may still respond to the former status.

front: {{c1::Social isolation}} is objectively having few contacts; {{c2::loneliness}} is the subjective distress of a gap between desired and actual connection.
back: They correlate only moderately: a person can be isolated without feeling lonely, or lonely in a crowd. Both independently predict elevated mortality, with meta-analytic effect sizes comparable to smoking, which is why screening should ask about both separately.

front: {{c1::Social loafing}} is reduced individual effort in groups when contributions are unidentifiable, e.g., slacking in a group project.
back: Loafing rises with group size and anonymity, and falls when tasks are evaluated individually or feel meaningful. Related size effects: diffusion of responsibility and the bystander effect.

front: {{c1::Transactional}} leadership exchanges rewards for performance; {{c2::transformational}} leadership motivates through vision and inspiration.
back: Transformational leadership predicts higher commitment and discretionary effort but can shade into dependence on a charismatic figure. Both differ from laissez-faire leadership, the absence of direction, which consistently predicts the poorest group outcomes.

front: A {{c1::dyad}} (Simmel) is the most intimate, least stable group; adding a member creates a {{c2::triad}}, allowing mediation and coalitions.
back: Simmel: the dyad dies if either member leaves, so each holds veto power and intimacy is maximal. The triad survives one exit and introduces new dynamics — two-against-one alliances and a mediator role.

front: A {{c1::master status}} overrides all others in how one is perceived — 'ex-convict', 'blind', 'celebrity', often 'physician'.
back: Master statuses can be ascribed or achieved, honored or stigmatized. Hughes's concept: it becomes the lens for every interaction, e.g., a wheelchair user finds disability treated as their defining trait.

front: A {{c1::primary}} group (Cooley) has intimate, enduring bonds valued in themselves (family); a {{c2::secondary}} group is impersonal and goal-directed.
back: Cooley coined primary group: face-to-face, long-term, ends in themselves, central to identity. Secondary groups (a chemistry class, coworkers) are instrumental and temporary — though they can evolve into primary ones.

front: A {{c1::reference}} group supplies the standards we use to evaluate ourselves, e.g., a premed measuring against admitted medical students.
back: Reference groups need not be groups we belong to — aspirational groups guide anticipatory socialization. Comparing to a better-off reference group produces relative deprivation even amid objective gains.

front: A hospital committee arrives at a more extreme decision than any member held alone. Name the phenomenon and both directions it can take.
back: Group polarization: discussion pushes the group toward the extreme of its initial average, producing a risky shift when members lean risky and a cautious shift when they lean cautious. The mechanisms are persuasive arguments and social comparison, not diffusion of responsibility.

front: A neighbor helps you move and you feel obliged to reciprocate. Which interaction theory explains this, and what norm enforces it?
back: Social exchange theory (Homans and Blau): interaction is analyzed as exchange of rewards and costs, and relationships persist while the ratio stays favorable relative to alternatives. The norm of reciprocity enforces repayment and creates standing obligation, so unreciprocated help strains ties.

front: A nurse must work the night of her daughter's recital, and also feels torn between speed and thoroughness on shift. Label each tension.
back: Work versus the recital is role conflict (nurse and parent are different statuses). Speed versus thoroughness is role strain (competing expectations within the single nurse role).

front: An {{c1::ascribed}} status is assigned involuntarily (race, sex, birth cohort); an {{c2::achieved}} status is earned (physician, felon, spouse).
back: Achieved statuses are not always desirable — 'felon' is achieved. Ascribed statuses can anchor stratification (caste). Most people occupy many of both at once (a status set).

front: An {{c1::in-group}} commands loyalty and a sense of 'we'; an {{c2::out-group}} is 'they', often viewed with competition or contempt.
back: In-group/out-group dynamics drive bias: favoring in-group members and homogenizing the out-group. Even arbitrary assignment creates loyalty, underpinning team spirit and prejudice alike.

front: Compare authoritarian, democratic, and laissez-faire leadership styles.
back: Authoritarian: leader decides alone — fast, fits crises, breeds resentment. Democratic: group participates — higher satisfaction, slower decisions. Laissez-faire: hands-off — works only with self-directed, expert members.

front: Compare the central and peripheral routes to persuasion.
back: Central: careful evaluation of argument quality, producing durable change. Peripheral: surface cues, producing fragile change.

front: Contrast Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft (Tonnies).
back: Gemeinschaft ('community'): bonds of kinship, place, and shared tradition — rural villages. Gesellschaft ('society'): impersonal, contractual, self-interested ties — modern cities. Parallels the primary/secondary group contrast.

front: Contrast groupthink and group polarization.
back: Groupthink suppresses dissent for harmony; group polarization strengthens members' pre-existing leanings.

front: Contrast instrumental and expressive leadership.
back: Instrumental leaders are task-oriented: goals, deadlines, efficiency. Expressive leaders are relationship-oriented: morale, cohesion, conflict-smoothing. Groups often informally split the two functions between people.

front: Describe cognitive dissonance and its resolution.
back: Discomfort from conflicting cognitions, resolved by changing an attitude or behavior to restore consistency (Festinger).

front: Describe front stage and back stage for a restaurant server.
back: Front stage: the dining room performance — smiles, scripted greetings, clean uniform, deference. Back stage: the kitchen — venting about customers, dropped posture, shared shortcuts. Goffman's dramaturgical model.

front: Distinguish a group from an aggregate and a category.
back: A group shares interaction and identity (a study group). An aggregate merely shares space (people at a bus stop). A category shares a trait without interaction (left-handers, O-negative donors).

front: Explain the bystander effect.
back: More bystanders means less helping, due to diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance.

front: Four types of social support: {{c1::emotional}} (empathy), instrumental (tangible aid), {{c2::informational}} (advice), and appraisal (feedback).
back: Matching matters: informational support helps most with controllable problems, emotional support with uncontrollable ones. A ride to dialysis is instrumental; a support group supplies emotional and appraisal support by showing how others in the same position are coping.

front: Garfinkel had students behave as boarders in their own homes, and families reacted with anger and alarm. What was he demonstrating?
back: Ethnomethodology: social order rests on taken-for-granted background expectancies that stay invisible until violated. Breaching experiments make norms visible by breaking them, showing that interaction is actively and continuously accomplished rather than merely following fixed rules.

front: Goffman: a {{c1::discredited}} stigma is already visible; a {{c2::discreditable}} one is concealable, making information control the central task.
back: A facial scar is discredited; HIV status or a psychiatric history is discreditable, forcing decisions about disclosure, passing, and covering. Courtesy stigma extends to associates, such as family members or clinicians who care for stigmatized patients.

front: How can a secondary group become a primary group?
back: Repeated instrumental contact can generate genuine attachment: coworkers or classmates begin as goal-oriented associates and develop enduring friendships valued for their own sake. The categories mark ends of a continuum.

front: How do mutual-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous work, analyzed sociologically rather than clinically?
back: They convert a discreditable stigma into a shared identity, supply a reference group carrying new norms, and use resocialization plus role modeling by members further along. The active mechanism is normative influence and identity change, not transfer of information.

front: Implicit bias in clinical settings can cause:
back:
**Differential treatment despite egalitarian intentions**

Documented in pain management disparities.

front: In dramaturgy (Goffman), the {{c1::front stage}} is where we perform a role for an audience; the {{c2::back stage}} is where the performance drops.
back: Goffman's Presentation of Self in Everyday Life: social life is theater. A server is polished in the dining room (front) and vents in the kitchen (back). Props, setting, and manner sustain the performance.

front: In hospital codes, the most effective fix for delayed action is assigning each task to a named person. Which two group processes does that counteract?
back: Diffusion of responsibility and social loafing: an unassigned task belongs to everyone and therefore to no one, and unidentifiable contributions reduce individual effort. Naming a person restores accountability and identifiability, the condition under which loafing disappears.

front: In Milgram's studies, obedience DECREASED when:
back:
**The experimenter was remote or the victim was close**

Proximity to consequences and distance from authority both reduced compliance.

front: Marx's four forms of alienation: from the {{c1::product}} of labor, from the {{c2::process}} of work, from other workers, and from one's human potential.
back: Alienation follows from lacking control over one's labor, not from disliking the job. Sociologists apply it to clinicians who lose control over pace, documentation, and clinical decisions, linking erosion of autonomy to burnout and to what is now called moral injury.

front: Name common dysfunctions of bureaucracy.
back: Red tape and rigidity, trained incapacity (rules followed even when counterproductive), goal displacement (means become ends), alienation of workers and clients, and oligarchy. Merton emphasized ritualist rule-following.

front: Name the concrete structural remedies Janis proposed to prevent groupthink.
back: Assign a devil's advocate, have the leader withhold his opinion at the outset, invite outside experts, split into independent subgroups that meet separately, and hold a second-chance meeting after a preliminary consensus. Each works by legitimizing dissent rather than by exhorting members to think harder.

front: Relative risk of 2.0 means the exposed group has:
back:
**Twice the risk of the unexposed group**

RR = 1.0 indicates no association.

front: Social loafing is:
back:
**Reduced individual effort in group tasks**

Reduced when individual contributions are identifiable.

front: Support predicts better health only among highly stressed people in one study but among everyone in another. Name the two competing hypotheses.
back: The stress-buffering hypothesis, in which support protects specifically by blunting appraisal and physiological reactivity to stressors, versus the direct or main effect hypothesis, in which integration benefits health regardless of stress. Perceived support usually buffers; structural integration usually shows main effects.

front: Symbolic interactionism focuses on:
back:
**How individuals create meaning through social interaction**

Symbolic interactionism (Mead, Blumer) is a micro-level sociological perspective that examines how people create meaning through symbols, language, and interaction in everyday life.

front: The {{c1::iron law of oligarchy}} (Michels): all large organizations, even democratic ones, drift toward rule by a small elite.
back: Michels argued leaders accumulate expertise, control of information, and communication channels, entrenching themselves. Seen in unions, parties, and associations originally built for member control.

front: The contact hypothesis states prejudice reduces when groups have contact that is:
back:
**Cooperative, equal-status, and institutionally supported**

Mere contact without these conditions can worsen prejudice.

front: The organizational chart says the attending decides, but the charge nurse effectively controls bed assignment. Name the distinction at work.
back: Formal versus informal organization: alongside official structure, informal networks, norms, and expertise-based influence determine how work actually gets done. Informal structure can raise efficiency or subvert stated goals, and it is entirely invisible on the formal chart.

front: Weber's ideal bureaucracy: division of labor, hierarchy of authority, written {{c1::rules}}, {{c2::impersonality}}, and merit-based hiring.
back: The five classic characteristics make large-scale coordination efficient and predictable. Weber also warned of the 'iron cage': rationalized systems trap individuals in rule-bound, disenchanted lives.

front: What are Etzioni's three types of formal organizations?
back: Utilitarian: joined for pay or credential (companies, universities). Normative or voluntary: joined for shared goals (charities, advocacy groups). Coercive: membership forced (prisons, psychiatric commitment), overlapping Goffman's total institutions.

front: What are the consequences of strong in-group identification?
back: In-group favoritism in rewards and trust, out-group homogeneity ('they're all alike'), scapegoating under threat, and double standards for judging identical acts. It builds solidarity while manufacturing prejudice.

front: What did Asch and Milgram each demonstrate?
back: Asch: conformity to an obviously wrong majority. Milgram: obedience to legitimate authority.

front: What did Weber mean by the 'iron cage'?
back: Rationalization and bureaucracy, once ascendant, imprison individuals in systems of efficiency, calculation, and rules, draining life of meaning and spontaneity — disenchantment. Ritzer's McDonaldization updates the idea.

front: What is a role set (Merton)?
back: The array of roles attached to a single status: a professor's role set includes teacher (to students), colleague (to faculty), employee (to administration), and mentor (to advisees). Competing role-set demands create strain.

front: What is a self-fulfilling prophecy in social interaction?
back: A false definition of a situation evokes behavior that makes it come true (Merton). Classic case: teachers told certain students were 'bloomers' treated them differently, and those students' performance rose (Rosenthal effect).

front: What is a voluntary (normative) association, and what functions does it serve?
back: An organization joined freely for shared purpose — Rotary, advocacy groups, congregational committees. Functions: pursuing collective goals, sociability, civic-skill building, and social capital (Putnam's concern in Bowling Alone).

front: What is face-work in Goffman's interaction theory?
back: Efforts to maintain one's own and others' 'face' — the positive social value claimed in interaction. Includes avoidance (dodging embarrassing topics) and corrective rituals (apologies, tactfully ignoring a gaffe).

front: What is goal displacement in organizations?
back: When adherence to rules and organizational self-preservation displace the original mission — a charity spending mainly on fundraising, or clinics optimizing documentation metrics over patient care. A classic bureaucratic pathology.

front: What is group polarization?
back: After discussion, groups shift toward more extreme versions of members' initial lean — riskier or more cautious. Driven by persuasive-arguments exposure and social comparison; visible in juries and online echo chambers.

front: What is social facilitation?
back: An audience improves performance on simple/well-learned tasks but impairs it on complex/novel ones.

front: What is stereotype threat?
back: Anxiety about confirming a negative stereotype consumes working memory and depresses performance.

front: What is the 'strength of weak ties' (Granovetter)?
back: Acquaintances (weak ties) bridge otherwise separate networks, so they carry novel information — job leads especially — that close friends, who share your contacts, cannot. Networks matter beyond intimacy.

front: What is the fundamental attribution error?
back: Overattributing others' behavior to disposition while underweighting the situation. The mirror image — explaining our own behavior situationally — is the **actor–observer bias**; the **self-serving bias** further credits our own successes to disposition and our failures to circumstance.

front: What is the relationship between status and role?
back: A status is a position in a social structure; a role is the behavior expected of that position. You occupy a status and play a role: 'medical student' is the status; studying and professionalism are the role.

front: What is the Thomas theorem?
back: 'If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences.' Subjective definitions drive behavior regardless of objective truth — a rumor of bank failure causes a real run. Basis of the self-fulfilling prophecy.

front: Which test compares means between two independent groups?
back:
**Independent t-test**

ANOVA extends this to three or more groups.

front: Why did Simmel consider triads more stable than dyads, despite dyads' greater intimacy?
back: A triad survives the loss of one member and disputes can be mediated by the third party; in a dyad, either member's exit destroys the group, so its existence depends continuously on both individuals.

front: Why do physicians and hospital administrators conflict structurally, in Weberian terms?
back: Professional authority rests on expertise and autonomous judgment over individual cases, while bureaucratic authority rests on rules, hierarchy, and standardization. Protocols, utilization review, and productivity targets sit on that fault line, a well-documented source of role strain and burnout.

front: Worker output at the Hawthorne plant rose whether the lighting was raised or lowered. Name the effect and the design lesson.
back: The Hawthorne effect: being observed and singled out changes behavior independent of the manipulation. It is a reactivity threat that requires a control group receiving equal attention. Later reanalyses suggest the original effect was smaller and partly driven by feedback and rest breaks.

front: {{c1::Allostatic load}} is cumulative physiological wear from chronic stress — a key mechanism linking low SES and discrimination to disease.
back: Repeated activation of stress systems (cortisol, catecholamines, inflammation) dysregulates cardiovascular, metabolic, and immune function. It offers a biological pathway from social position to hypertension and diabetes.

front: {{c1::Compliance}} implies patient obedience, {{c2::adherence}} implies an agreed plan, and concordance describes shared decision-making about the regimen.
back: Nonadherence is predicted far more by regimen complexity, cost, side effects, asymptomatic disease, depression, and poor clinician communication than by patient motivation or intelligence. Roughly half of patients with chronic disease deviate from their regimen, so it is the norm, not an anomaly.

front: {{c1::Food deserts}} are areas with poor access to affordable nutritious food, concentrating diet-related disease in low-income and rural communities.
back: A structural, not behavioral, explanation of diet: with only convenience stores and fast food nearby, 'choices' are constrained. Related concept: food swamps, where unhealthy options dominate healthy ones.

front: {{c1::Fundamental cause}} theory (Link and Phelan): SES stays linked to disease across eras because money, knowledge, and networks are flexible resources.
back: As old proximate risks are solved (sanitation), the advantaged deploy resources against new ones (statins, screening), regenerating the gradient. Implication: intervening on mechanisms alone never closes the gap.

front: {{c1::Illness experience}} is the interactionist study of how people manage symptoms, meaning, and identity — central in chronic disease.
back: Chronic illness can cause biographical disruption: renegotiating work, relationships, and self-concept. Patients actively interpret symptoms, seek legitimacy for contested conditions, and manage stigma and disclosure.

front: {{c1::Incidence}} counts new cases arising over a period; {{c2::prevalence}} counts all existing cases at a point in time.
back: Prevalence rises with both incidence and duration, so a treatment that extends life without curing raises prevalence while incidence is unchanged. Incidence is the right measure for studying causes and evaluating prevention; prevalence is the right measure for planning services and staffing.

front: {{c1::Lead-time}} bias lengthens measured survival by diagnosing earlier; {{c2::length}} bias makes screening oversample slow-growing disease.
back: Together they can produce longer survival after diagnosis with no reduction in deaths, and overdiagnosis is length bias in the extreme. This is why mortality rate, not five-year survival, is the valid endpoint for evaluating a screening program.

front: {{c1::Medicalization}} turns nonmedical problems into illnesses (ADHD, baldness); {{c2::demedicalization}} reverses it — homosexuality left the DSM in 1973.
back: Conrad's framework: pharmaceutical marketing, physician authority, insurers, and advocacy groups drive medicalization. It can legitimate suffering and unlock treatment, but also pathologizes normal variation and expands social control.

front: {{c1::Medicare}} covers people 65 and older plus those with ESRD or disability; {{c2::Medicaid}} is joint federal-state coverage based on income.
back: Because Medicaid is state-administered, eligibility and reimbursement vary widely, and states declining ACA expansion left a coverage gap for adults earning too much for Medicaid but too little for exchange subsidies. Low reimbursement also limits which clinicians accept it.

front: {{c1::Single-payer}} means one entity pays for privately delivered care; {{c2::socialized medicine}} means government also owns facilities and staff.
back: Universal coverage is the broader goal of insuring everyone by any mechanism, including regulated private insurance. Canada illustrates single-payer, the UK NHS and the US Veterans Health Administration illustrate socialized delivery, and the US overall has neither.

front: {{c1::Social epidemiology}} studies how social structure — class, race, gender, place — distributes disease and mortality across populations.
back: It shifts the question from individual risk factors to the causes of the causes: why exposure and vulnerability are patterned. Core tools: gradients, neighborhood effects, and measures like allostatic load.

front: A {{c1::DALY}} counts years of healthy life lost to illness and premature death; a {{c2::QALY}} weights years of life gained by their quality.
back: DALYs are used to quantify burden of disease and set public health priorities; QALYs are used in cost-effectiveness analysis of specific interventions. Both attach explicit numeric value to health states, which is why disability weights are ethically contested, particularly by disability advocates.

front: A study finds higher hypertension rates among Black patients and concludes there is a genetic cause. What is the interpretive error?
back: Race is a social category that proxies for exposure to discrimination, segregation, income, diet environment, and care access, so unmeasured social confounding is far more plausible than genetic causation. Genetic ancestry does not align with racial categories, and within-group variation exceeds between-group variation.

front: Ajzen's theory of planned behavior predicts intention from three components. Name them and the model's main limitation.
back: Attitude toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. Its limitation is the intention-behavior gap: intention explains only part of behavior, because habits, environments, and competing demands operate outside conscious intention entirely.

front: An uninsured woman in labor arrives at an emergency department. Which law governs the response, and what does it fail to cover?
back: EMTALA requires screening and stabilization regardless of ability to pay at any hospital participating in Medicare. It is an unfunded mandate limited to emergencies, covering neither follow-up, medications, nor chronic care, which is why emergency departments absorb unmet primary care demand.

front: Being {{c1::uninsured}} or underinsured predicts delayed care, skipped medications, fewer screenings, and later-stage diagnoses.
back: Cost is the classic access barrier, but underinsurance (high deductibles, narrow networks) produces similar delay. Later-stage cancer diagnosis among the uninsured is a signature disparity finding.

front: Beyond cost, what barriers limit healthcare access?
back: Insurance gaps and narrow networks, transportation and distance, inflexible work hours, childcare, language and interpretation, low health literacy, provider shortages, discrimination, and distrust rooted in past abuses.

front: Case and Deaton documented rising midlife mortality among less-educated Americans from three causes. Name them and the proposed mechanism.
back: Suicide, drug overdose, and alcohol-related liver disease, collectively called deaths of despair.
